newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook - Copper to swing on inventory data.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook - Copper to swing on inventory data.

text.p: Copper prices are set for a lively week on the London Metal Exchange (LME), with the twice-weekly warehouse inventory report likely to be the focus of attention.
Analysts said the key will be whether a long run of drawdowns that has left LME stocks at six-year lows continues.

"Any signs that metal is moving back into LME warehouses, especially Singapore, would likely pressure prices lower as this would confirm widespread rumours that Chinese-held copper was being returned to the market," LME trader Brandeis said.
Last Friday, copper stocks dropped by 8,650 tonnes to 123,700, but there were 1,100 tonnes delivered into Singapore.

Since the beginning of September, over 150,000 tonnes of copper has left the LME's warehouses without interruption. This metal is moving to take advantage of attractive arbitrage opportunities in the U.S. and China, some said.
But arbitrage operations are fickle and can quickly become uneconomic, so the drawdowns reflect exploding physical demand prompted by low prices since the Sumitomo scandal, others said.

"The physical copper market is strong, low availability of scrap and delayed exports from the CIS have meant that discounts on scrap and off-grade metal are now trading at flat or even a slight premium," William Adams of LME trader Rudolf Wolff said.

The main uncertainty is China -- and whether the Chinese are shipping metal for consumption, in which case it will eventually be custom-cleared and show in import figures. If it stays in bonded warehouses there it can easily return to the world market.

"I would not like to say where we will be (this week). It (the market) could rise or fall $50 overnight, and if there is a big arrival in Singapore you could see a bloodbath," a senior trader at an LME ring dealer said.
November traded options are declared Wednesday, and recent monthly expiries have been preceded by volatile LME swings.
Last week copper prices ranged between $2,042 and $1,900 a tonne, ending Friday's kerb session at $1,958.
Chart analysts said the close above $1,955 was constructive and threw up the possibility of an advance towards $1,990/2,000.
The rest of the complex was likely to be dependent on copper, although zinc should continue to show spirit after ending last week near 5-1/2 month highs of $1,075.
Zinc soared on investment fund buying, spurred by talk that international financier George Soros had entered the market.
Technical analysts were pencilling in $1,090 as a target but pointing out a chart gap just below $1,042.
The aluminium market might be restrained if there are strikes at various General Motors facilities, as the automotive industry is a major end-user, traders said.

Prices finished at $1,425 on Friday after classic technical action over the week between $1,399 and $1,455. However, they would be vulnerable to a test of $1,400/1,410 if the market cannot run up and tackle $1,450 again, chartists said.
Trading in tin, lead and nickel was unlikely to throw up any fireworks. --London Newsroom, +44 171 542 8080
